why: §5.5 forbids either implementation from carrying a table of its own or asking its
language for a character class. Nothing in the real corpus can prove that: Python's
isalpha() and JavaScript's \p{L} agree on every character the corpus contains, so a
port that asks the language passes every real vector and is wrong only on characters
no test file has. This asset settles it by construction. Every class here
CONTRADICTS what any language built-in would say -- 7 is a letter, z is a digit, '.'
is whitespace and ' ' is not, ',' is symbolic and '+' is not -- so an implementation
that consults a built-in, in either direction, diverges on the first case.
Every expected value below was derived from §5.1, §5.2 and §5.4 by hand and checked
against both implementations; none was copied from a run. Measured: these cases
catch all twelve single-field substitutions of the forbidden kinds, in both
languages. Read `subtokens`, which under D21 is the only level that is indexed.

cases.why: z is a digit here, and a digit CONTINUES an identifier (§5.2)
7 is a letter here; a port asking the language splits it out
z starts a NUMERIC run, which a quasi-letter does not continue; a port that thinks z is a letter gets ['z','z']
9 continues the identifier, then §5.4 splits on it as a separator
a maximal run of digits is one token (§5.2)
9 is a RENDERED digit, excluded from a numeric run, and each is kept by §5.4's fallback clause
the rendered digit ends the numeric run rather than joining it
the real space is NOT whitespace here, so it is a token of its own
'.' IS whitespace here: discarded, and a boundary
'!' is the discarded character here (D4's role, played by a different character)
'?' is NOT discarded here; a port with D4 hard-coded drops it
',' is the ASCII-symbolic class here, so a run of them is one token
'+' is NOT symbolic here; a port with D8's set hard-coded merges them
'%' is a quasi-letter AND a separator: it continues the identifier, then splits it
'_' is a quasi-letter here but NOT a separator; a port with '_.' hard-coded splits it
§5.4's fallback clause: a token made entirely of rendered characters survives whole
the same clause, for the rendered digit
step 3a converts the escape the symbol table defines
step 3a converts, then step 3b folds the pair @z the fold table defines
an escape the table does not define stays literal, and none of \ < > is symbolic here

step 3b is non-overlapping: @ is a marker, @% is not in the table, both are consumed, so %1 never folds. A port whose marker set is written out by hand rather than read off the fold table folds it and gets ['x','@','P']
the same parity, with the other marker
and the pair the table does define folds
